newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Child burial sparks debate on immigrants in Belgium.
newsitem.headline: Child burial sparks debate on immigrants in Belgium.

text.p: The burial at the weekend of a young Belgian-born Moroccan girl has reopened racial and political schisms over the rights and social integration of immigrants in linguistically divided Belgium.

The issue has been around since the 1970s. But it has failed consistently to find the political consensus needed even to pass into law the provisions of the 1992 Maastricht treaty on the local voting rights of other European Union citizens.

The death of Loubna Benaissa, nine years old when she disappeared in August 1992 and whose body was found a week ago stuffed in a steel trunk in the basement of a Brussels garage, has reignited the debate with a vengeance.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, a Flemish Christian Democrat, admitted on Sunday that mistakes had been made.
Asked if racism had hindered the investigation, he said: "I hope that's not what we will discover - from time to time I fear it played a part."

The parents of some of the four other Belgian girls whose bodies have been found since August in Belgium's paedophile rape and murder scandal, told the 20,000 mourners at Loubna's funeral on Saturday their suffering had crossed racial barriers.

Dehaene chose the voting issue to highlight the need to integrate not only the 140,000 Moslems living in Belgium but also the many other religions and races among the country's 10 million inhabitants.
"It is a key point in the integration of immigrants," he said on Sunday, carefully choosing simply to hand the matter to parliament without further guidance.
The debate even includes whether to allow special cemeteries for Moslems, following the decision of Loubna's parents to fly her body back to Morocco for burial.
But it is the voting issue, which requires a change in the constitution, that has grabbed the headlines since the weekend and sparked the political debate.

Flemish parties have blocked the passing into law of the Maastricht treaty provisions giving voting rights to nationals of other EU nations resident in Belgium out of fear that this would swing the balance in favour of their Francophone compatriots.
For them, granting voting rights to other foreigners is even further out of the question.
The radical Flemish party Vlaams Blok accused Dehaene of trying to capitalise on the death of a young girl to shoehorn through contentious legislation.

Herman De Croo, leader of the Flemish Liberal Party, the biggest opposition party, said on Monday there should be no granting of voting rights to residents from non-EU nations unless they took Belgian nationality.
It was a point of view echoed to varying degrees by Dehaene's own party and the Francophone Liberals (PRL).
"The exercise of voting rights goes hand-in-hand with adherence to the laws of a nation, and the best way of demonstrating such adherence is naturalisation," PRL President Louis Michel said.
The Flemish Vlaams Unie agreed with this point of view but added that obtaining citizenship should not be easy.

But Agalev, the Flemish Green Party, took the view that voting rights were fundamental to social integration and that the constitution should be quickly adapted, a stand echoed by the National Committee for Universal Suffrage.

The Francophone Christian Democrats (PSC) and the Francophone Socialists (PS) -- who together with Dehaene's VLD and the Flemish Socialists (SP) form Belgium's centre-left coalition government -- sat on the fence.
"It wouldn't be good to create two types of foreigners," said PS member and Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo.
